deep.reconstruction:
Context (cote 154, 1983-84): Grothendieck is building a combinatorial 'space' Γ(Σ) of arrangements (systems) of pseudo-lines. Vertices D are configuration types. Edges are elementary degenerations: a specialization, where a triangle of the arrangement collapses to a triple point; its inverse, a generalization; and 'pseudo-specializations'. Around each vertex D he forms a link polygon Pol*(D). Its vertices are the edges of Γ(Σ) at D, and its edges carry a 'gradation' (an integer or angle-like weight). On the next page Γ(Σ) is called a 'grapho-variété'.

For a specialization D→D' there is a morphism Pol*(D)→Pol*(D'), a 'restriction/specialization' map. The previous page showed this map is generally not an isomorphism: some vertices (a, a') of Pol*(D') are missing from the image.

This page first states the compatibility condition in that case. Suppose b is a vertex of Pol*(D') that is missing in Pol*(D). Suppose b lies on the arc from a to x in Pol*(D'), where x is the other neighbour of b. Then a and x are adjacent in Pol*(D). The gradation of the edge ax in Pol*(D) must equal grad(xb) + grad(ba) computed in Pol*(D'). The transcription writes Pol*(D) for both sides; logically the right-hand side lives in Pol*(D'). So gradations are additive under subdivision.

In a bracketed aside he says this should be formalised by a notion of the induced gradation on a sub-polygon of a graded polygon. It should be set up so that the 'déploiements' (unfoldings) of the initial graded polygons and of their sub-polygons commute. He then asks whether the restriction maps Pol*(D)→Pol*(D') are already determined by the other structures on Γ(Σ): orientation of edges (specialization vs. generalization) and gradation.

Section 12 begins a systematic review of the structure of Pol*(D) for non-critical D. Its vertices (= edges of Γ(Σ) at D) fall into three kinds:
- specialization vertices: edges leaving D;
- generalization vertices: edges arriving at D;
- neutral vertices: edges that are 'linked' or unoriented at D.

There is an antipodal involution on Pol*(D). He records:
- (a) some class of vertices (probably the generalization vertices) is stable under antipody;
- (b) the antipode of a specialization vertex is a specialization vertex;
- (c) a characterization of a vertex that is not a specialization vertex but is the antipode of one. It is equivalent to being adjacent to two generalization vertices such that the edge joining them has gradation zero, and conversely.

The next page completes the programme. The orientation of vertices of Pol*(D) is recovered from the specialization morphisms. Conversely, those morphisms are recovered from the cyclic order, their effect on one orientation, and the image of a distinguished vertex as the antipode of (D',α). He also observes that around 2-cells the local polygons form a local system on the underlying surface.

Purpose: an intrinsic, purely combinatorial axiomatization of the local structure (links plus specialization maps) of the stratified space of pseudo-line arrangements.
errors: Gap, not an error: the gradation additivity is stated as a necessary condition ('on doit avoir') without definition of gradation or proof; the notion of induced gradation on a sub-polygon is explicitly left undeveloped.
Item (a) of the list is garbled or incomplete; the precise statement about which vertex class is antipody-stable cannot be confirmed from the page.
Characterization (c) is asserted without argument; it is plausible but unverifiable from this page alone.

ideas.what: Link polygons Pol*(D) at each vertex of a combinatorial complex Γ(Σ) of pseudo-line arrangement types, with specialization morphisms between links along degeneration edges
ideas.modern_name: Links of strata in a stratified (combinatorial) moduli space; exit-path/specialization maps between links; flip graph of pseudoline arrangements and its 2-dimensional cell structure (higher Bruhat orders B(n,2), combinatorial Grassmannian/MacPhersonian)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Ringel (1956, flip connectivity); Manin–Schechtman (1986-89, higher Bruhat orders); MacPherson (1993, combinatorial differential manifolds/MacPhersonian); exit-path categories: MacPherson, Treumann, Lurie (2000s)
ideas.where_published: Pseudo-lines not treated in EGA/SGA; Esquisse d'un programme (1984) discusses tame topology and polygon/moduli combinatorics, but I am unsure whether it mentions pseudo-line systems explicitly.

ideas.what: Additivity of edge gradations under the non-isomorphic specialization map (a missing vertex subdivides an edge, and gradations add)
ideas.modern_name: Compatibility of weights/angles under subdivision; functoriality of a graded link under refinement

ideas.what: Request for a theory of graded sub-polygons whose 'unfoldings' (déploiements) commute with inclusion
ideas.modern_name: Functorial developing/unfolding of graded polygons (akin to developing maps of polyhedral structures, or graded cyclic orders)

ideas.what: Classification of link vertices as specialization / generalization / neutral, an antipodal involution on the link, and a characterization of antipodes via zero-gradation edges
ideas.modern_name: Local orientation data on links of a stratified space; antipodal symmetry of the link (cf. the link of a codimension-2 stratum in an arrangement space being a polygon with central symmetry, e.g. zonogon/octagon faces of B(n,2))
ideas.usually_credited_to: implicit in work on higher Bruhat orders and zonotopal tilings (Ziegler 1993; Felsner–Weil)

ideas.what: Reconstruction question: are the specialization morphisms between links determined by orientation plus gradation of Γ(Σ)?
ideas.modern_name: Recovering the exit-path/stratification structure from the underlying graded oriented complex

missed.claim: Grothendieck proposes axiomatizing the local structure of the space of pseudo-line arrangements as graded link polygons with specialization morphisms and antipodal involutions. He asks whether the specialization morphisms are recoverable from orientation and gradation alone. The next page sketches a yes. This intrinsic-local-structure programme for the arrangement 'grapho-variété' does not appear as such in the oriented-matroid or higher-Bruhat literature.
missed.quote: La question se pose si les restrictions Pol*(D) → Pol*(D') se déduisent des autres structures de Γ(Σ) (orientation et gradation)
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It amounts to asking for an exit-path-category/stratified-space description of pseudoline-arrangement moduli recovered from combinatorial data. That is relevant to realization spaces, MacPhersonian topology, and constructible sheaves on combinatorial stratifications.

missed.claim: The page combines link polygons, antipody and gradation with the next page's 'local system' of local polygons over 2-cells. Together these implicitly treat the flip complex of pseudoline arrangements as a stratified space carrying a constructible local system of links. This anticipates exit-path/constructible viewpoints that were later applied to arrangement spaces mostly independently.
missed.quote: il faudrait développer la notion de gradation dans un sous-polygone d'un polygone gradué..., de telles façons que les déploiements des polygones gradués initiaux et sous-polygones, soient commutatifs
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is a historical precedent rather than a new theorem. It might interest people studying the topology of combinatorial Grassmannians or the 2-dimensional structure of higher Bruhat orders.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a fragmentary working page inside an unpublished programme. The overall programme (an intrinsic combinatorial 'grapho-variété' of pseudoline arrangements with link polygons and specialization maps) is historically interesting and little known. The specific content here, however (gradation additivity and a classification of link vertices), is routine bookkeeping without a finished result.
transcription_corrections: Line 1: 'Si b n'est que [?] dans Pol*(D)' should read 'Si b manque dans Pol*(D)', consistent with the previous page's 'sommets ... qui manquent'.
'gradation des â,x dans Pol*(D) = somme des gradations des x̂b, b̂a dans Pol*(D)': the second occurrence should be Pol*(D'), since b exists only in Pol*(D'). The image appears to show Pol*(D').
'(en dessous [?] D non critique)' is more likely '(en supposant D non critique)' or '(en dehors de D critique)'.
'les arêtes de généralisation (ce sont elles arrivant à D)' is better read as 'ce sont celles arrivant à D'.
In item c), 'adjacent à [deux] sommets' reads in the image as 'adjacent à deux sommets de généralisation'.
